To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The N-terminal domain of the prion (PrP) is a powerful toxicity transducer that is regulated in cis by its C-terminus and that this mechanism is disrupted in neurotoxic PrP mutants and in PrPSc, a toxic isoform of PrP.
the N-terminal domain of prion protein is the effector of toxicity that is tightly regulated by the globular domain.

the N-terminal domain of prion protein is an effector that transduces toxicity and its activity is regulated in cis by its interaction with the globular C-terminus, which is a novel auto-inhibition mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cellular prion protein PrPC, a protein found on the surface of all mammalian neurons.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the neurotoxicity of prion diseases.
understanding the cellular mechanisms that underlie the neurodegenerative diseases caused by the misfolding of prion protein.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the C-terminal domain is a negative regulator of the N-terminal domain, and that PrPC is a protein with two distinct domains with opposing functional properties.
the N-termini of PrPC and PrPSc are the key toxic effectors that mediate the neurotoxicity of the prion disease.
the N-terminal domain of the prion is a toxic efflector, whose activity is tightly controlled in cis by the C-terminal domain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PrPC, the normal isoform of the cellular prion protein, is an auto-inhibited, ionic current-generating effector that is regulated by the globular, C-terminal domain.
the C-termini of the prion proteins, both the cellular (PrPC) and infectious (PrPSc) isoforms, are critical for regulating the activity of the N-terminal domains of the prion.
the prion protein has a toxic effector that can be activated by anti-PrP antibodies and that is regulated by the globular domain of PrP.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the prion protein has two functional domains that are in constant competition with each other, with the flexible N-terminal domain being a toxic effector that is normally kept in check by the globular domain.
PrP toxicity is regulated in cis by intramolecular interactions between the N- and C-termini.
the N-terminally located flexible region of PrPC functions to mediate the neurotoxicity of PrPSc.
